bib.title: AdapterDrop: On the Efficiency of Adapters in Transformers
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), pages 7930-7946

read.skipped: Figure-only numeric axes and the bulk of tables 9-12 and figure data were skimmed, not transcribed; reference list skimmed for lineage

question: How computationally efficient are adapters (Houlsby, Pfeiffer) and AdapterFusion at training and inference time versus full fine-tuning, and can adapters be dropped or pruned to make them faster with little loss?
hypothesis: Adapters in lower transformer layers matter little for task performance, so removing them (and pruning rarely-activated adapters in AdapterFusion) cuts compute with minimal accuracy loss.
contributions: First establishment of the computational efficiency of adapters vs full fine-tuning: training steps up to 60% faster, inference 4-6% slower
AdapterDrop: dynamic removal of adapters from lower layers, specialized and robust variants, with large multi-task inference speedups
AdapterFusion pruning: remove least-activated adapters after fusion training, keeping task performance

method.summary: Timing of BERT-base-configuration transformers with full fine-tuning, Houlsby and Pfeiffer adapters (AdapterHub) on V100 and Titan X GPUs; AdapterDrop (adapters removed from the first n layers, trained with fixed n or random n per batch) evaluated on GLUE with RoBERTa-base; AdapterFusion layer removal and adapter pruning evaluated on small GLUE tasks.
method.task: Efficiency of adapter-based fine-tuning and inference; GLUE classification/regression

datasets.name: GLUE (excluding WNLI)
datasets.split: dev sets; SST-2, MNLI, QNLI, QQP trained 10 epochs, the rest 20 epochs

datasets.name: English Wikipedia dump (adapter MLM pre-training, Appendix B)
datasets.size: 250k steps at batch 64, no sentence used twice

models.name: RoBERTa-base + Pfeiffer adapter
models.architecture: transformer encoder with adapters; compression (reduction) rate 16 default

other.note: inferred: 12 layers from n drawn from [0, 11]

models.name: AdapterFusion (8 adapters, one per GLUE task)
models.architecture: attention-style fusion of task adapters per layer

training.regularisation: Robust AdapterDrop: n drawn randomly from [0, 11] per batch; AF dropout 0-75% (Appendix E)
training.hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 PCIe 32GB and Titan X Pascal 12GB (timing only)
training.seeds: three runs, mean and std of best dev score after each epoch

other.hyperparameters: default adapter fine-tuning hyperparameters of Pfeiffer et al. 2021a, values not printed

inference.samples: timing: each step repeated 300 times, median reported

parameters.af_pruning: keep adapters with highest average activation per fusion layer, activations averaged over the AF training set

metrics.name: Relative speed
metrics.definition: S_a / S_f (adapter vs full fine-tuning); 1.5 means 1.5 steps in the time of one full-FT step

metrics.name: Speedup
metrics.definition: p% means adapter model with AdapterDrop needs (1-p/100)x runtime; additive per dropped layer

metrics.name: GLUE dev score
metrics.definition: task metrics (accuracy, Spearman, MCC etc.); also reported as % of standard adapter

baselines: standard adapter with no dropped layers
eval.protocol: timing median of 300 repeats on two GPUs, torch.cuda.Event with synchronize; task scores mean of 3 runs

evidence.quote: default hyperparameters for adapter ﬁne-tuning as in (Pfeiffer et al., 2021a)

results.claim: Adapter training steps are up to 60% faster than full fine-tuning (Pfeiffer, seq 128, batch 32 = 1.60).
results.setup: BERT-base config, V100, seq 128, batch 32, Pfeiffer adapter
results.quote: Adapters can be considerably faster compared to full model ﬁne-tuning—60% faster

results.claim: Houlsby adapter training relative speed at seq 512 batch 32.
results.note: Speedup shrinks with larger inputs (1.33-1.37 at 512/32); Pfeiffer 1.37

results.claim: Adapter inference is 94-96% as fast as fully fine-tuned models (4-6% slower).
results.setup: BERT-base config, Houlsby and Pfeiffer, V100 and Titan X

results.claim: Adapters need no more training steps to converge than full fine-tuning, and MLM pre-training of adapters gives no convergence gain.
results.setup: RoBERTa-base, 8 GLUE tasks, Pfeiffer adapter, MLM pre-training on Wikipedia 250k steps batch 64

results.claim: Each shared transformer layer speeds up multi-task inference by up to 8.4% (16 simultaneous tasks).
results.setup: Multi-task inference, 16 simultaneous tasks; average over batch sizes 16, 32, 64, seq 128

results.claim: With adapters dropped from the first five layers, inference on 8 tasks at once is 39% faster.
results.setup: Multi-task inference, 8 simultaneous tasks, first five layers dropped
results.quote:
with adapters
dropped from the ﬁrst ﬁve layers, AdapterDrop
is 39% faster

results.claim: Dropping the first five layers gives inference speedups of 21-42% depending on number of simultaneous tasks.
results.quote: we measure inference speedups of 21–42% with ﬁve

results.claim: Specialized AdapterDrop with five dropped layers retains 97.1% of the standard adapter's average GLUE performance.
results.setup: RoBERTa-base, 8 GLUE tasks, separate model trained per n, 5 layers dropped
results.table: Table 8, row Specialized AdapterDrop (12 models), column 5

results.claim: Robust AdapterDrop with five dropped layers retains 95.4% of average GLUE performance (one model for all n).
results.setup: RoBERTa-base, 8 GLUE tasks, n drawn from [0,11] per batch
results.note: Robust model at 0 dropped layers retains 98.5; at 11 dropped 62.0; specialized at 11 is 82.9

results.claim: A standard adapter (trained with no dropped layers) degrades to 89.0% with five layers dropped at test time, so AdapterDrop training is what makes dropping safe.
results.setup: RoBERTa-base, 8 GLUE tasks, dropping at evaluation only

AF with

results.claim: AdapterFusion pruning to two remaining adapters (of eight) matches the full AF models and improves inference speed by 68%.

With two remaining adapters, we achieve
comparable results to the full AF models with eight

results.note: Table 3 shows 8-adapter AF inference at 0.38 of full FT versus 2-adapter 0.64, consistent with the order of magnitude

results.claim: Per dropped AdapterFusion layer speedup, inference with 16 adapters.
results.note: Training V100 for 16 adapters is 7.8%; for 8 adapters 5.2% inference, 7.3% training

results.note: Text says 74%; Table 7 prints 73.7%. MRPC improves 88.4 -> 89.3

results.claim: Cross-layer parameter sharing at compression rate 16 costs 2.35% average GLUE score (85.35 to 83.0) with 74k params; rate 4 uses 295k params, 66% fewer than standard 884k.
results.setup: RoBERTa-base, Pfeiffer architecture, shared adapter weights across layers
results.note: Rate 4 average 84.39; shared adapter at rate 16 needs only 307KB storage

limits: Speed measured only on BERT-base configuration with V100 and Titan X GPUs, PyTorch 1.5.1, small encoder models; no decoder-only or billion-parameter LLMs
Accuracy experiments use GLUE dev sets with RoBERTa-base only, mean of three runs
Authors say AdapterDrop might not be suitable for all tasks; CoLA drops sharply and RTE/CoLA fall steeply even with AdapterDrop
Multi-task speedup only applies when several independent predictions are made on the same input
Adapters are 4-6% slower at inference than full fine-tuning
Parallel AdapterFusion implementation (convolution reformulation) gave no gain; iterative is faster at larger inputs
Training speedups depend on input size; CUDA cores are the bottleneck
Authors call Appendix B-E results preliminary
Optimizer, learning rate and adapter hyperparameters are not printed (refer to Pfeiffer et al. 2021a); no code link in text
